relationship: rain sought from the Lord rather than other powers
rationale: Zechariah commands asking the Lord for seasonal rain and says He gives winter rain and vegetation. Jeremiah likewise asks whether idols can bring rain and looks to the Lord as maker of these things. Both locate the sought rainfall in His agency.
source_text: Ask the Lord for rain in its season, early and late. The Lord made appearances and will give them winter rain, to each person vegetation in the field.

target_units.text: Is there among the nations’ idols one who brings rain? Can heaven give its fullness? Is it not Thou Thyself? And we will wait for Thee, because Thou madest all these things.

relationship: false visions and empty assurances mislead the people
rationale: Zechariah condemns diviners' false visions, false dreams and vain comfort before describing the people's distress. Ezekiel likewise condemns false visions and vain divinations that mislead the people with declarations of peace when none exists. Both expose deceptive religious reassurance.
source_text: For those making pronouncements spoke troubles, the diviners false visions; they were telling false dreams and giving vain comfort. Therefore they were carried away like sheep and mistreated, because there was no healing.

target_units.text: They see false things and divine vain things, those who say, ‘The Lord says,’ although the Lord has not sent them; and they began to establish a word.
Have you not seen a false vision and spoken vain divinations?
Therefore say, ‘Thus says the Lord: Because your words are false and your divinations vain, therefore behold, I am against you, says the Lord,

and I will stretch out My hand against the prophets who see false things and utter vain things. They will not belong to My people’s instruction, nor be written in the register of the house of Israel, nor enter Israel’s land. They will know that I am the Lord.
Because they misled My people, saying, ‘Peace, peace,’ when there was no peace, and this one builds a wall, and they coat it—if it is going to fall,

relationship: judgment of shepherds joined to renewed care for the flock
rationale: Zechariah announces wrath against shepherds and the Lord's attention to His flock, Judah's house. Jeremiah likewise condemns shepherds who scatter the sheep and promises gathering and renewed shepherding. Both contrast failed leadership with divine care for the people.
source_text: My wrath was provoked against the shepherds, and I will attend to the lambs. The Lord God Almighty will attend to His flock, Judah’s house, and make them like His splendid horse in battle.

target_units.text: O shepherds who scatter and destroy the sheep of My pasture!
Therefore thus says the Lord to those shepherding My people: You scattered My sheep and drove them out without visiting them. Behold, I am exacting justice from you according to your evil practices.
And I will receive the remnant of My people from all the land where I drove them out, and establish them in their pasture; they will increase and multiply.
And I will raise shepherds for them who will tend them, and they will no longer fear or be frightened, says the Lord.

relationship: confidence in the Lord contrasted with defeated horse power
rationale: Zechariah's fighters prevail because the Lord is with them, while horse riders are shamed. The psalm likewise contrasts reliance on chariots and horses with magnification in the Lord's name and describes the opponents falling. Both make the Lord, rather than cavalry, decisive.
source_text: They will be like fighters trampling mud in the roads in battle; they will draw up for combat because the Lord is with them, and horse riders will be put to shame.

target_units.text: These rely on chariots, and those on horses, but we will be magnified in the name of the Lord our God.
They were fettered and fell, but we rose and were set upright.

relationship: Judah and Joseph included together in divine restoration
rationale: Zechariah promises strength for Judah and salvation for Joseph, followed by settlement and renewed relation to their God. Ezekiel likewise brings Joseph and Judah together, gathers Israel into the land and promises that they will be His people and He their God. Both explicitly include these named houses in restoration.
source_text: I will strengthen Judah’s house and save Joseph’s house. I will settle them because I have loved them; they will be as though I had not turned them away, for I am the Lord their God and will listen to them.

target_units.text: say to them, Thus says the Lord: Behold, I will take Joseph’s tribe through Ephraim’s hand, and Israel’s tribes attached to him, and place them upon Judah’s tribe. They will become one staff in Judah’s hand.
The staffs upon which you wrote will be in your hand before them,

and say to them, Thus says the Lord, the Lord: Behold, I am taking all Israel’s house from among the nations where they entered, gathering them from all those around them and bringing them into Israel’s land.
I will make them one nation in My land and upon Israel’s mountains, and one ruler will be theirs. They will no longer be two nations or ever again be divided into two kingdoms,

so that they no longer defile themselves with their idols. I will deliver them from all their lawless deeds in which they sinned and cleanse them. They will be My people, and I, the Lord, will be their God.

relationship: Judah and Israel gathered within restored belonging to God
rationale: Zechariah promises restoring Judah and Joseph as though not rejected. Hosea likewise reverses the declaration 'not My people' and announces Judah and Israel gathering together. Both combine the named people's restoration with reversal of alienation, using their respective house names.
source_text: I will strengthen Judah’s house and save Joseph’s house. I will settle them because I have loved them; they will be as though I had not turned them away, for I am the Lord their God and will listen to them.

target_units.text: The number of Israel’s sons was like the sand of the sea, which will not be measured or counted. In the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not My people,’ there they will be called sons of the living God.
Judah’s sons and Israel’s sons will gather together, appoint one authority for themselves and come up from the land, for great is Jezreel’s day.
Say to your brother, ‘My People,’ and to your sister, ‘Shown Mercy.’

relationship: wine used to describe a gladdened human heart
rationale: Zechariah compares Ephraim's rejoicing heart with the effect of wine. The psalm directly says wine gladdens the human heart. The particular wine-and-heart association explains the comparison, without turning Zechariah's promised joy into a command to drink.
source_text: They will be like Ephraim’s fighters, and their heart will rejoice as with wine. Their children will see and be glad; their heart will rejoice in the Lord.

target_units.text: and wine gladdens the human heart, to brighten the face with oil, and bread makes the human heart firm.

relationship: a divine signal followed by gathering the scattered people
rationale: Zechariah promises the Lord's signal and reception of the redeemed people. Isaiah likewise describes His raised signal and gathering of Israel's lost and Judah's scattered ones. Both expressly connect signaling with gathering.
source_text: I will signal to them and receive them, for I will redeem them; they will multiply as they were once many.

target_units.text: He will raise a signal to the nations and gather Israel’s lost ones; He will gather Judah’s scattered ones from the earth’s four wings.

relationship: remembrance and return while dispersed among peoples
rationale: Zechariah describes those sown among peoples remembering God from far away and returning with their children. Deuteronomy likewise speaks of taking the Lord's words to heart among the nations of dispersion, returning to Him and being gathered. Both place inward recollection and return within exile.
source_text: I will sow them among peoples, and those far away will remember Me; they will nourish their children and return.

target_units.text: And it shall be, when all these things come upon you, the blessing and the curse which I have set before your face, and you receive them into your heart among all the nations whither the Lord has scattered you,
and you return unto the Lord your God, and obey His voice according to all that I command you this day, with all your heart and with all your soul,
then the Lord shall heal your sins, and have mercy upon you, and shall gather you again from all the nations whither the Lord has scattered you.

relationship: recovery of the remnant from Egypt and the Assyrians
rationale: Zechariah promises bringing the people back from Egypt and receiving them from the Assyrians. Isaiah likewise names the Assyrians and Egypt among the places from which the remaining people are recovered and gathered. The named regions provide the particular connection.
source_text: I will bring them back from Egypt’s land and receive them from the Assyrians. I will bring them into Gilead and Lebanon, and not even one of them will be left behind.

target_units.text: On that day the Lord will again show His hand, to be zealous for the remaining remnant of the people left from the Assyrians, Egypt, Babylonia, Ethiopia, the Elamites, the sun’s rising and Arabia.
He will raise a signal to the nations and gather Israel’s lost ones; He will gather Judah’s scattered ones from the earth’s four wings.

relationship: waters made passable in the people's return
rationale: Zechariah describes passage through a narrow sea, struck waves and dried river depths while foreign domination is removed. Isaiah likewise describes Egypt's sea laid waste and a river struck so that the remnant can pass through in sandals. Both join altered waters with return, preserving their distinct geography and actions.
source_text: They will pass through a narrow sea and strike waves in the sea; all the rivers’ depths will dry up. All the Assyrians’ arrogance will be removed, and Egypt’s scepter will be taken away.

target_units.text: The Lord will lay Egypt’s sea waste and bring His hand upon the river with a violent wind. He will strike seven ravines so that one may pass through it in sandals.
There will be a passage for My remaining people in Egypt, and it will be for Israel as on the day it came out of Egypt’s land.

relationship: strength and exaltation associated with the Lord's name
rationale: Zechariah promises strength in the Lord and boasting in His name. The psalm likewise describes His saving strength and says the people will be magnified in the Lord their God's name. Both place the people's confidence in Him rather than their own resources.
source_text: I will strengthen them in the Lord their God, and they will boast in His name, says the Lord.

target_units.text: Now I know that the Lord saved His anointed; He will hear him from His holy heaven; in mighty acts is the salvation of His right hand.
These rely on chariots, and those on horses, but we will be magnified in the name of the Lord our God.
They were fettered and fell, but we rose and were set upright.

relationship: Lebanon and cedars consumed in announced judgment
rationale: Zechariah calls Lebanon to open its doors for fire to devour its cedars. Jeremiah likewise addresses Judah's royal house with Lebanon imagery and announces its chosen cedars cut down and thrown into fire. The shared Lebanon, cedar and fire imagery is explicit, with different addressed settings.
source_text: Open your doors, Lebanon, and let fire devour your cedars!

target_units.text: Because thus says the Lord against the house of Judah’s king: You are Gilead to Me, the head of Lebanon; surely I will make you a wilderness, cities that will not be inhabited.
And I will bring against you a destroying man and his axe, and they will cut down your chosen cedars and cast them into the fire.

relationship: the fall of Lebanon's cedars and Bashan's oaks
rationale: Zechariah calls for lament over the fallen cedar and devastated Bashan oaks. Isaiah likewise includes the high cedars of Lebanon and oaks of Bashan among those reached by the Lord's humbling day. The two named kinds and places connect the imagery.
source_text: Let the pine wail, for the cedar has fallen, because the mighty have suffered greatly! Wail, Bashan’s oaks, for the thick-grown forest has been torn down!

target_units.text: For the Lord Sabaoth has a day against every insolent and arrogant person, against everyone high and elevated; they will be humbled,
against every cedar of Lebanon among the high and elevated, and against every oak tree of Bashan,

relationship: shepherds lament the destruction of their greatness and pasture
rationale: Zechariah reports shepherds lamenting their afflicted greatness alongside roaring lions. Jeremiah likewise commands shepherds to mourn and reports their cries because the Lord destroyed their grazing places. The shared shepherd-lament scene is particular, without equating every accompanying image.
source_text: A sound of shepherds lamenting, for their greatness has suffered! A sound of lions roaring, for the Jordan’s proud swelling has suffered!

target_units.text: Raise a shout, shepherds, and cry out; beat yourselves in mourning, rams of the sheep, because your days for slaughter have been fulfilled, and you will fall like choice rams.
And flight will perish from the shepherds, and salvation from the rams of the sheep.
A sound of shepherds crying and of sheep and rams shouting, because the Lord destroyed their grazing places,

relationship: a flock marked for slaughter
rationale: Zechariah commands shepherding sheep destined for slaughter. Jeremiah likewise addresses shepherds and rams as their days for slaughter arrive and escape fails. Both present a doomed flock, though one begins a symbolic shepherding action and the other commands mourning.
source_text: Thus says the Lord Almighty: “Shepherd the sheep destined for slaughter,

target_units.text: Raise a shout, shepherds, and cry out; beat yourselves in mourning, rams of the sheep, because your days for slaughter have been fulfilled, and you will fall like choice rams.
And flight will perish from the shepherds, and salvation from the rams of the sheep.

relationship: shepherds profit from a flock they fail to care for
rationale: Zechariah describes buyers slaughtering sheep, sellers rejoicing in wealth and shepherds feeling nothing for them. Ezekiel likewise condemns shepherds who consume the flock's products and slaughter fattened animals without feeding or healing the sheep. Both indict exploitation joined to failed care.
source_text: which their buyers were slaughtering without regret; their sellers said, ‘Blessed be the Lord; we have become rich!’ Their shepherds felt nothing for them.

target_units.text: “Son of man, prophesy against Israel’s shepherds. Prophesy and say to the shepherds, ‘Thus says the Lord, the Lord: O shepherds of Israel, surely shepherds do not feed themselves? Do shepherds not feed the sheep?
Behold, you consume the milk, clothe yourselves with the wool and slaughter the fattened animal, but you do not feed My sheep.
You have not strengthened the weak, restored the sick to health, bound up the broken, brought back the wandering or sought the lost. You have worn down the strong with toil.

relationship: same-book people handed over against their neighbors
rationale: Zechariah 11 announces each person being handed into a neighbor's and a king's hands as the land is cut apart. Chapter 8 likewise describes a period when God sends everyone against his neighbor and travel has no peace. The mutual hostility within the land links the judgments.
source_text: Therefore I will no longer spare the land’s residents, says the Lord. Look, I am handing over human beings, each into his neighbor’s hands and his king’s hands. They will cut the land to pieces, and I will certainly not rescue from their hand.”

target_units.text: Before those days people’s wages will bring no benefit, and animals’ hire will not exist; those going out or coming in will have no peace because of affliction. I will send everyone out against his neighbor.

relationship: same-chapter two named staffs enacted as symbols of broken relations
rationale: The shepherd takes the staffs Beauty and Measuring Cord. The later actions discard the beautiful staff to dissolve a covenant and the second staff to dissolve the possession between Judah and Israel. The named objects explicitly connect their introduction with their subsequent symbolic actions.
source_text: I will shepherd the sheep destined for slaughter into Canaan’s land. I will take two staffs for myself—I called one Beauty and the other Measuring Cord—and I will shepherd the sheep.

target_units.text: I will take my beautiful staff and throw it away, to dissolve my covenant that I made with all the peoples.
It will be dissolved on that day, and the Canaanites—the sheep being guarded—will know that it is the Lord’s word.
I will say to them, “If it is good before you, weigh out and give my wages, or refuse.” They weighed out my wages: thirty silver pieces.

The Lord said to me, “Put them into the smelting furnace and examine whether it is approved, as I was tested on their behalf.” I took the thirty silver pieces and threw them into the Lord’s house, into the smelting furnace.
I threw away the second staff, Measuring Cord, to dissolve the possession between Judah and Israel.

relationship: neighbors consuming one another's flesh under judgment
rationale: Zechariah announces refusal to shepherd and says the remaining people will devour their neighbors' flesh. Jeremiah likewise announces each eating his neighbor's flesh during siege, alongside the flesh of children. The severe image is shared, while siege is explicit in Jeremiah.
source_text: I said, “I will not shepherd you. Let the dying die, and let the failing fail; let those remaining each devour his neighbor’s flesh.”

target_units.text: And they will eat the flesh of their sons and daughters, and each will eat his neighbor’s flesh in the encirclement and siege with which their enemies will besiege them.
